meta.description: Not Gandhi. There is no record of him saying it; the closest documented source is a 1918 union speech by Nicholas Klein, and the popular wording is a 1980s paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Gandhi. The closest documented antecedent is Nicholas Klein's 1918 union speech; the four-stage 'then you win' wording is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — closest documented source is Nicholas Klein (1918)
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Gandhi ever saying or writing this. The earliest strong match is a May 1918 speech by union lawyer Nicholas Klein to the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America: “First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.” The tidy four-stage “then you win” wording is a later paraphrase, and it was not attached to Gandhi’s name until 1982 — decades after his death. Treat the exact popular sentence as an anonymous modern paraphrase.

source.excerpt: First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive support” for ascribing the saying to Gandhi, who died in 1948.
The earliest strong match is a 1918 speech by union lawyer Nicholas Klein ↗ to the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America — ending “they build monuments to you,” not “then you win.”
The Gandhi link surfaces only in 1982, when WIN magazine ↗ summarized his philosophy as “first they ignore you; then they abuse you; then they crack down on you and then you win.”
The idea belongs to an older family of “stages of a new truth” sayings; Schopenhauer ↗ voiced a related version in 1819.
source.excerptNote: Nicholas Klein’s actual 1918 words — note that they end with “build monuments to you,” not “then you win,” and never mention Gandhi.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular sentence is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no single identifiable author, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. Nicholas Klein’s underlying 1918 speech would itself be public domain in the US, but its wording differs materially from the quote as circulated.

author.name: Nicholas Klein
author.heading: Who was Nicholas Klein?
author.bio: Nicholas Klein (1884–1951) was a Cincinnati-born labor attorney and union advocate who began as a reporter for a socialist magazine before earning his law degree in 1910. Addressing the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America in Baltimore in May 1918, he predicted the union’s trajectory in the four-stage line now routinely and wrongly credited to Gandhi. He later served on Cincinnati City Council and as vice mayor.

misattribution.heading: How Gandhi got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely shared “Gandhi” quotes online — and he almost certainly never said it. Researchers have combed his collected works without finding it.

items.why: No version of “first they ignore you … then you win” has been located in Gandhi’s writings or speeches; Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive support” for the attribution.
Klein told the Amalgamated Clothing Workers ↗: “First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.”

Activist Peter D. Jones paraphrased Gandhi’s philosophy as “first they ignore you; then they abuse you; then they crack down on you and then you win,” the first documented Gandhi linkage — 34 years after his death, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment belongs to an old lineage of “stages of a new truth” sayings and the closest wording is Nicholas Klein’s, not Gandhi’s — the crisp “then you win” version is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line compresses a whole theory of social change into four beats: an idea is dismissed, mocked, resisted, and finally triumphant. That arc feels true to anyone in a movement, which is exactly why it spreads — and why a famous nonviolence icon like Gandhi is such a magnetic (if unearned) name to hang it on.

Ironically, its documented root is not spiritual but industrial: a union lawyer rallying garment workers in 1918, promising that the labor movement they were building would one day be honored with monuments.
context.pull: Klein said they would “build monuments to you” — the “then you win” came later, from other hands.
